title: Default unreleased projects to replacement and state reset, then review migration policy after first release
body:
## Outcome

Add a reviewed project policy for legacy migration and compatibility, keyed to whether the target project has ever actually been released. Before any release, the default is to replace obsolete persistent-state formats and APIs directly, reset affected project-owned user state, and remove obsolete compatibility code instead of maintaining migrations from unreleased versions. Once a first release exists, prompt the user to revise the policy before further incompatible changes or state resets.

## Why this matters

Requested by the current user: migration from never-released versions wastes implementation effort, increases codebase complexity, and leaves stale state that can generate misleading bug reports. This supports the charter's minimal-babysitting outcome and explicit human control while reducing unnecessary compatibility work.

## Acceptance criteria

- Initialization and policy review expose a plain-language legacy migration policy with release-history evidence, default provenance, user overrides, and review history.
- For a project confirmed never released, default to direct replacement of old persistent schemas, APIs, and interfaces; reset affected project-owned state so development and testing start from the current state contract. Do not create migration chains, adapters, or dual-format support merely to preserve unreleased behavior. Document intentional state loss.
- Reset behavior is bounded to the affected project's obsolete state; it must not remove unrelated user files or state. This policy does not bypass higher-authority safety, destructive-operation, or deployment boundaries.
- Execution, capture, bootstrap, and relevant cleanup/refactoring guidance consistently honor the reviewed policy. An unreleased project's stale-state fixture is replaced/reset and obsolete API paths are removed rather than migrated.
- Detect the first actual release through evidenced project release conventions, rather than inferring it from a version string alone. When release history is uncertain, request clarification during interactive review or persist a decision blocker during unattended execution before treating state as disposable.
- After a first release, mark the pre-release policy as needing review and prompt the user to choose a suitable compatibility and data-preservation policy. Unattended execution records this as a durable blocker for affected incompatible changes; it does not wait for a user or silently keep wiping state.
- The chosen post-release policy is recorded and enforced. Do not prescribe a universal migration strategy or silently overwrite an existing explicit user policy; repeated checks of the same reviewed release transition do not produce duplicate prompts.
- Focused policy and workflow verification covers never-released defaults, explicit overrides, affected-state reset scope, stale-state false-positive prevention, released projects, first-release transition, uncertain release history, and review persistence. Update shared documentation and generated supported distributions; required prompt-budget checks pass.

## Scope and constraints

Implement the reusable policy model, release-history evidence and transition handling, review presentation, workflow guidance, and focused verification in ZzzOps. This goal does not authorize wiping this repository's current data or retroactively declaring released versions unsupported. Live execution was subsequently requested; release and current-project data-wipe authority remain unchanged.

## Relationships and first probe

No duplicate outcome found in the complete portfolio. Completed policy-provenance and rigor goals supply existing mechanisms, not dependencies. Inspect policy defaults, reviewed override handling, release evidence, destructive-operation boundaries, and current migration guidance. Use disposable unreleased/released project fixtures to show whether the proposed policy can distinguish replace/reset from preserve/review without guessing release history. Identify ambiguous prerelease or private-distribution conventions as explicit review questions if repository evidence cannot resolve them.

Stop the first chunk when the release-evidence and policy-transition contract is falsifiably demonstrated, or persist a categorized blocker if the boundaries cannot be established. Do not build a generic migration engine.

## Design decision required before implementation

Proposed release-evidence contract for user review:

- An actual published distribution counts as released, including prereleases and private releases.
- Native published-release or registry evidence proves a release exists. Confirmed project conventions may supply other publication evidence.
- Never-released status requires an explicit owner declaration recorded in reviewed policy. Empty release listings, absent tags, and version strings alone cannot establish that status.
- Missing, unavailable, or conflicting evidence is unknown; block only affected incompatible changes or resets.
- Existing reviewed projects remain usable and are never silently opted into resets. The first release makes a pre-release policy need review. Once the user approves a released-project policy, later releases do not repeat that first-release prompt.
- Reset scope is affected project-owned state; external/deployed resets retain existing external-write and deployment authority requirements.

The reviewed project policy disables automated design, so B-001 requests approval of this contract or changes to it before adding the durable policy model. Implementation will use existing policy provenance, review-table, digest and history mechanisms, with bounded release-evidence acquisition and focused never-released/released/unknown fixtures. No generic migration engine or current-project state wipe is proposed.
